claim: The same build-to-threshold decision variable signal that triggers an initial choice continues to evolve after commitment.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that the same build-to-threshold decision variable signal that triggers an initial choice continues to evolve after commitment, and determines the timing and accuracy of self-initiated error detection reports by selectively representing accumulated evidence that the preceding choice was incorrect.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental EEG data showing CPP dynamics before and after decision commitment.

claim: The post-decision accumulation signal determines the timing and accuracy of self-initiated error detection reports.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that the same build-to-threshold decision variable signal that triggers an initial choice continues to evolve after commitment, and determines the timing and accuracy of self-initiated error detection reports by selectively representing accumulated evidence that the preceding choice was incorrect.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by analyses showing relationships between CPP build-up rate and error detection timing.

claim: The post-decision signal selectively represents accumulated evidence that the preceding choice was incorrect.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that the same build-to-threshold decision variable signal that triggers an initial choice continues to evolve after commitment, and determines the timing and accuracy of self-initiated error detection reports by selectively representing accumulated evidence that the preceding choice was incorrect.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by data showing CPP increases after detected errors but not after correct responses or undetected errors.

claim: A peri-choice signal generated in medial frontal cortex provides a source of input to the post-decision accumulation process.
source: We also show that a peri-choice signal generated in medial frontal cortex provides a source of input to this post-decision accumulation process, indicating that metacognitive judgments are not solely based on the accumulation of feedforward sensory evidence.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by mediation analysis showing FCθ influences CPP build-up rate.

claim: Metacognitive judgments are not solely based on the accumulation of feedforward sensory evidence.
source: We also show that a peri-choice signal generated in medial frontal cortex provides a source of input to this post-decision accumulation process, indicating that metacognitive judgments are not solely based on the accumulation of feedforward sensory evidence.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion based on the finding that medial frontal signals influence post-decision accumulation.

claim: Categorical choices are thought to be made by integrating evidence over time into a decision variable that triggers action upon reaching a criterion.
source: Categorical choices are thought to be made by integrating evidence over time into a decision variable that triggers action upon reaching a criterion (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Kelly and O'Connell, 2014; Shadlen and Kiani, 2013; Smith and Ratcliff, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on decision-making.

claim: Most theoretical models of metacognition propose that the same decision variable makes a key contribution to internal representations of choice accuracy.
source: Most theoretical models of metacognition propose that the same decision variable makes a key contribution to internal representations of choice accuracy (de Martino et al., 2013; Heath, 1984; Kiani et al., 2014; Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Link, 2003; Moran et al., 2015; Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Ratcliff and Starns, 2013; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple theoretical models in the literature.

claim: Human participants can retrospectively categorize certain choices as erroneous even in the absence of external feedback.
source: However, the specification that the decision variable reaches a fixed threshold prior to commitment means that these models cannot account for the fact that human participants can retrospectively categorize certain choices as erroneous even in the absence of external feedback (Rabbitt and Vyas, 1981; Rabbitt, 1966; Yeung et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies demonstrating error detection without feedback.

claim: Alternative theoretical models have been proposed in which metacognitive judgments can exploit additional evidence that is accumulated after first-order commitment.
source: To take account of this kind of observation, alternative theoretical models have been proposed in which metacognitive judgments can exploit additional evidence that is accumulated after first-order commitment (Moran et al., 2015; Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models proposing post-decisional accumulation.

claim: A definitive neurophysiological demonstration of post-decisional evidence accumulation has yet to be definitively provided in humans or other animals.
source: However, a definitive neurophysiological demonstration of post-decisional evidence accumulation has yet to be definitively provided in humans or other animals.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature identified by the authors based on their review.

claim: Subjects successfully withheld from responding on an average of 56.6% (±13.0) of No-Go trials.
source: Subjects successfully withheld from responding on an average of 56.6% (±13.0) of No-Go trials, and 68.0% (±16.7) of erroneous presses were followed by an error detection report (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral performance data from the experiment, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: 68.0% (±16.7) of erroneous presses were followed by an error detection report.
source: Subjects successfully withheld from responding on an average of 56.6% (±13.0) of No-Go trials, and 68.0% (±16.7) of erroneous presses were followed by an error detection report (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral performance data from the experiment, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Primary RT and RTd were not correlated across detected error trials.
source: Primary RT and RTd were not correlated across detected error trials (mean within-subject β = −0.05, s.e.m. = 0.04; t27 = −1.4, p = 0.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data showing no significant correlation.

claim: The median primary RTs for detected errors (457 ± 21 ms) were faster than correct Go RTs (511 ± 22 ms).
source: The median primary RTs for detected errors (457 ± 21 ms) were faster than correct Go RTs (511 ± 22 ms; t27 = 5.5, p < 1 x 10−4), whereas undetected errors were significantly slower than Go RTs (543 ± 28 ms; t27 = 2.9, p = 0.007; detected vs. undetected errors: t27 = 5.8, p < 1 x 10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of reaction time data across trial types.

claim: Undetected errors were significantly slower than Go RTs (543 ± 28 ms).
source: The median primary RTs for detected errors (457 ± 21 ms) were faster than correct Go RTs (511 ± 22 ms; t27 = 5.5, p < 1 x 10−4), whereas undetected errors were significantly slower than Go RTs (543 ± 28 ms; t27 = 2.9, p = 0.007; detected vs. undetected errors: t27 = 5.8, p < 1 x 10−4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of reaction time data across trial types.

claim: The CPP exhibited a gradual build-up with a rate that was inversely proportional to RT.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015), the CPP exhibited a gradual build-up with a rate that was inversely proportional to RT, and reached a stereotyped amplitude at the time of first-order choice commitment (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of EEG data shown in Figure 2a and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: The CPP reached a stereotyped amplitude at the time of first-order choice commitment.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015), the CPP exhibited a gradual build-up with a rate that was inversely proportional to RT, and reached a stereotyped amplitude at the time of first-order choice commitment (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of EEG data shown in Figure 2a and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: The CPP exhibited persistent post-commitment build-up on a subset of trials, continuing its positive trajectory prior to an error detection report.
source: Despite the fact that the median RTd was executed 560 ms after stimulus offset, precluding the continued integration of feedforward sensory evidence in the period preceding error detection, the CPP exhibited persistent post-commitment build-up on a subset of trials, continuing its positive trajectory prior to an error detection report but gradually diminishing in amplitude following Go decisions and undetected errors (Figure 2b; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for explicit comparison of signals on Go and undetected error trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data analysis shown in Figure 2b demonstrating continued CPP evolution after decision commitment.

claim: Second-order performance could be reliably classified as early as 120 ms prior to error commission.
source: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis (see Materials and methods) conducted in discrete temporal windows along the entire signal time course revealed that second-order performance could be reliably classified as early as 120 ms prior to error commission (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis of the CPP signal shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The build-up rate of the second-order CPP was steeper on trials characterized by faster error detection.
source: Mirroring our observations for the first-order responses, the build-up rate of the second-order CPP was steeper on trials characterized by faster error detection, and it again reached a fixed amplitude immediately prior to the error detection report (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of CPP dynamics sorted by error detection RT, shown in Figures 2d and 2e.

claim: The second-order CPP reached a fixed amplitude immediately prior to the error detection report.
source: Mirroring our observations for the first-order responses, the build-up rate of the second-order CPP was steeper on trials characterized by faster error detection, and it again reached a fixed amplitude immediately prior to the error detection report (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of CPP dynamics sorted by error detection RT, shown in Figures 2d and 2e.

claim: Error detection decisions were based on the selective accumulation of internal evidence that the previous choice was incorrect.
source: Thus, rather than reflecting a continuation of the first-order decision process, these data suggest that error detection decisions were based on the selective accumulation of internal evidence that the previous choice was incorrect.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the second-order CPP only increased after detected errors and not after correct responses or undetected errors.

claim: The posterior medial frontal cortex (pMFC) is highly responsive to variations in performance accuracy.
source: A substantial literature incorporating several species and modes of neurophysiological measurement has established that the posterior medial frontal cortex (pMFC) is highly responsive to variations in performance accuracy (Carter et al., 1998; Ito et al., 2003; Narayanan et al., 2013; Ridderinkhof et al., 2004) and its activity predicts neural and behavioral adaptation following error commission (Cavanagh et al., 2009; Danielmeier et al., 2011; Ebitz and Platt, 2015; Narayanan et al., 2013; Sheth et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies across species and measurement modalities.

claim: pMFC activity predicts neural and behavioral adaptation following error commission.
source: A substantial literature incorporating several species and modes of neurophysiological measurement has established that the posterior medial frontal cortex (pMFC) is highly responsive to variations in performance accuracy (Carter et al., 1998; Ito et al., 2003; Narayanan et al., 2013; Ridderinkhof et al., 2004) and its activity predicts neural and behavioral adaptation following error commission (Cavanagh et al., 2009; Danielmeier et al., 2011; Ebitz and Platt, 2015; Narayanan et al., 2013; Sheth et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies demonstrating predictive relationships between pMFC activity and post-error adaptation.

claim: FCθ underwent a sharp positive deflection at approximately the time of errors that were subsequently detected.
source: The time-course of FCθ did not distinguish between correct Go responses and undetected errors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) but underwent a sharp positive deflection at approximately the time of errors that were subsequently detected (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of FCθ power time-courses shown in Figure 3b.

claim: ROC analysis applied to single-trial FCθ waveforms revealed strong detection-predictive activity that achieved significant detection classification up to 120 ms before initial error commission.
source: ROC analysis applied to single-trial FCθ waveforms revealed strong detection-predictive activity that, as with the CPP, achieved significant detection classification up to 120 ms before initial error commission (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis of FCθ shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Pre-response FCθ power was consistently lower on trials with faster first-order RTs.
source: In keeping with previous observations (Cavanagh et al., 2011; Cohen and Donner, 2013), pre-response FCθ power was consistently lower on trials with faster first-order RTs (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of FCθ sorted by RT shown in Figure 3d and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: Fast error detections were preceded by greater FCθ power.
source: A reliable relationship also existed between pre-detection FCθ on detected errors and RTd, but here fast error detections were preceded by greater FCθ power (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of FCθ sorted by error detection RT shown in Figures 3e and 3f.

claim: Single-trial FCθ power was strongly negatively related to RTd.
source: As expected, single-trial FCθ power was strongly negatively related to RTd (t27 = –7.2, p < 1 x 10−6).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial regression analysis showing a significant negative relationship.

claim: The pre-detection amplitude of the second-order CPP did not reliably correlate with RTd.
source: In contrast, the pre-detection amplitude of the second-order CPP did not reliably correlate with RTd (t27 = −1.9, p = 0.08; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), consistent with the aforementioned observation of a threshold-crossing effect prior to error detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial regression analysis showing no significant correlation.

claim: FCθ power was a better predictor of RTd than CPP amplitude.
source: Statistical comparison of the associated regression weights indicated that FCθ power was a better predictor of RTd than CPP amplitude (t27 = 3.3, p = 0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of regression coefficients from single-trial analyses.

claim: CPP build-up rate robustly predicted RTd.
source: The opposite pattern was apparent for the build-up rates and peak latencies of both signals: CPP build-up rate (t27 = -−5.0, p < 1 x 10−4) and latency (t27 = 4.9, p < 1 x 10–4, derived by permutation testing; see Materials and methods) robustly predicted RTd with both effects maximal over centro-parietal scalp (Figure 4b,c), whereas these features of the FCθ signal did not reliably account for trial-by-trial variance in RTd (build-up rate: t27 = –1.9, p = 0.07; latency: t27 = –0.7, p = 0.5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial regression analysis showing significant prediction of RTd by CPP build-up rate.

claim: CPP peak latency robustly predicted RTd.
source: The opposite pattern was apparent for the build-up rates and peak latencies of both signals: CPP build-up rate (t27 = -−5.0, p < 1 x 10−4) and latency (t27 = 4.9, p < 1 x 10–4, derived by permutation testing; see Materials and methods) robustly predicted RTd with both effects maximal over centro-parietal scalp (Figure 4b,c), whereas these features of the FCθ signal did not reliably account for trial-by-trial variance in RTd (build-up rate: t27 = –1.9, p = 0.07; latency: t27 = –0.7, p = 0.5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial regression analysis showing significant prediction of RTd by CPP peak latency.

claim: FCθ build-up rate and latency did not reliably account for trial-by-trial variance in RTd.
source: The opposite pattern was apparent for the build-up rates and peak latencies of both signals: CPP build-up rate (t27 = -−5.0, p < 1 x 10−4) and latency (t27 = 4.9, p < 1 x 10–4, derived by permutation testing; see Materials and methods) robustly predicted RTd with both effects maximal over centro-parietal scalp (Figure 4b,c), whereas these features of the FCθ signal did not reliably account for trial-by-trial variance in RTd (build-up rate: t27 = –1.9, p = 0.07; latency: t27 = –0.7, p = 0.5; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-trial regression analysis showing no significant prediction of RTd by FCθ build-up rate or latency.

claim: FCθ power began to reliably predict the speed of error detection approximately 350 ms before the CPP did.
source: First, FCθ power began to reliably predict the speed of error detection approximately 350 ms before the CPP did (compare Figures 2d and 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ROC analysis time-courses for FCθ and CPP shown in Figures 2d and 3c.

claim: FCθ was a reliable predictor of CPP build-up rate in a mediation model.
source: FCθ was a reliable predictor of CPP build-up rate in this model (p = 0.0007) and the mediation effect was significant (p = 0.0009), indicating that the rate of second-order evidence accumulation partially mediated the observed relationship between medial frontal signaling and the speed of error detection (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by path analysis showing a significant relationship between FCθ and CPP build-up rate.

claim: The rate of second-order evidence accumulation partially mediated the observed relationship between medial frontal signaling and the speed of error detection.
source: FCθ was a reliable predictor of CPP build-up rate in this model (p = 0.0007) and the mediation effect was significant (p = 0.0009), indicating that the rate of second-order evidence accumulation partially mediated the observed relationship between medial frontal signaling and the speed of error detection (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis showing CPP build-up rate mediates the FCθ-RTd relationship.

claim: The one-choice drift diffusion model fit the error detection data well.
source: The model fit the error detection data well, capturing the shapes of the group-level and single-subject RTd distributions (Figure 6b; Table 1; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) as well as the considerable heterogeneity in individuals' capacities for accurate second-order evaluation (Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative model fitting results shown in Figure 6b, Table 1, and Figure 6c.

claim: The temporal evolution of the simulated decision variable time-series closely traced that of the second-order CPP.
source: Despite minimal data-driven constraint on the simulation process (see Materials and methods), the temporal evolution of the simulated time-series closely traced that of the second-order CPP (Figure 6d).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulated decision variables and observed CPP waveforms shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Drift ratio was positively correlated with FCθ power across subjects.
source: We employed the per-subject 'drift ratio' (v/η) as a model-based estimate of each individual's error evidence strength (Ratcliff and Van Dongen, 2011; Materials and methods) and found that this quantity was positively correlated with FCθ power (r = 0.51, p = 0.007; Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by between-subjects correlation analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Drift ratio was correlated with the build-up rate of the second-order CPP across subjects.
source: Conversely, drift ratio was correlated with the build-up rate (r = 0.47, p = 0.013; Figure 6f) and peak latency (r = −0.52, p = 0.005; Figure 6g) of the second-order CPP, whereas no such relationships were observed for FCθ build-up rate (βFCθ = −0.12, p = 0.53; βCPP = 0.46, p = 0.017) or latency (βFCθ = −0.10, p = 0.64; βCPP = −0.46, p = 0.042).
evidence: This claim is supported by between-subjects correlation analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Drift ratio was correlated with the peak latency of the second-order CPP across subjects.
source: Conversely, drift ratio was correlated with the build-up rate (r = 0.47, p = 0.013; Figure 6f) and peak latency (r = −0.52, p = 0.005; Figure 6g) of the second-order CPP, whereas no such relationships were observed for FCθ build-up rate (βFCθ = −0.12, p = 0.53; βCPP = 0.46, p = 0.017) or latency (βFCθ = −0.10, p = 0.64; βCPP = −0.46, p = 0.042).
evidence: This claim is supported by between-subjects correlation analysis shown in Figure 6g.

claim: FCθ and the CPP were clearly observed following 'no-report' errors.
source: Finally, we asked a new cohort of 12 subjects to perform the same Go/No-Go task but gave no instructions to report errors on half of the task blocks. FCθ and the CPP were clearly observed following these 'no-report' errors and, consistent with the fact that no-report blocks contain a mixture of detected and undetected errors, linear contrasts confirmed that FCθ and second-order CPP amplitudes were intermediate between their amplitudes following detected and undetected errors in the condition with self-initiated error reporting (FCθ, t11 = 4.2, p = 0.002; CPP, t11 = 6.9, p < 1 x 10–4; Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of a new cohort performing a no-report version of the task, shown in Figure 7.

claim: FCθ and second-order CPP amplitudes in no-report blocks were intermediate between their amplitudes following detected and undetected errors in the condition with self-initiated error reporting.
source: FCθ and the CPP were clearly observed following these 'no-report' errors and, consistent with the fact that no-report blocks contain a mixture of detected and undetected errors, linear contrasts confirmed that FCθ and second-order CPP amplitudes were intermediate between their amplitudes following detected and undetected errors in the condition with self-initiated error reporting (FCθ, t11 = 4.2, p = 0.002; CPP, t11 = 6.9, p < 1 x 10–4; Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of signal amplitudes across conditions shown in Figure 7.

claim: The close relationship between the second-order CPP and error detection signalling cannot be attributed to motor preparation or execution.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that the close relationship between the second-order CPP and error detection signalling cannot be attributed to motor preparation or execution.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including dissociation from motor signals, topographic stability, and observation in no-report conditions.

claim: The CPP that precedes a first-order perceptual decision is fully dissociable from motor preparation signals.
source: First, we have previously shown that the CPP that precedes a first-order perceptual decision is fully dissociable from motor preparation signals and is observed even when no overt decision-reporting action is required (O'Connell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: There was no change in signal topography between the pre- and post-choice phases.
source: Second, we observed no change in signal topography between the pre- and post-choice phases (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by topographic analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: If the decision-maker is allowed to report delayed, self-initiated judgments of their own performance, these judgments will incorporate new internal information available after the point of commitment.
source: Our results reveal that if the decision-maker is allowed to report delayed, self-initiated judgments of their own performance, these judgments will incorporate new internal information available after the point of commitment, even in the absence of continued sensory input.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing post-decision CPP accumulation.

claim: The present findings represent the first definitive neurophysiological demonstration of post-decision evidence accumulation.
source: Our findings, however, represent the first definitive neurophysiological demonstration of post-decision evidence accumulation.
evidence: This claim is an assertion by the authors about the novelty of their findings based on their review of the literature.

claim: The first-order task required subjects to discriminate between the two possible stimulus categories (i.e. Go versus No-Go).
source: The first-order task required subjects to discriminate between the two possible stimulus categories (i.e. Go versus No-Go), a process that can be understood in terms of competitive accumulation of evidence in favor of each choice alternative (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Gomez et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim describes the task design and is supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: The CPP builds in response to evidence favoring each of the choice alternatives in competitive accumulation contexts.
source: We have previously shown that the CPP builds in response to evidence favoring each of the choice alternatives in such contexts (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012) and accordingly, we observed here that the same signal exhibited a gradual build-up prior to both Go and No-go choices.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors and current observations.

claim: The second-order task was more comparable to simple signal detection with detected errors translating to hits and undetected errors translating to misses.
source: The second-order task, by contrast, was more comparable to simple signal detection with detected errors translating to hits and undetected errors translating to misses.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the task structure by the authors.

claim: Human decision-makers are capable of quickly engaging multiple decision processes in succession that are reliant on the same neural mechanism of evidence integration but are constructed in qualitatively distinct ways.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that human decision-makers are capable of quickly engaging multiple decision processes in succession that, although reliant on the same neural mechanism of evidence integration, are constructed in qualitatively distinct ways.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation of different CPP dynamics for first- and second-order decisions.

claim: Peri-response FCθ power was strongly predictive of subsequent error detection.
source: First, peri-response FCθ power was strongly predictive of subsequent error detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROC analysis and regression analyses showing FCθ predicts error detection.

claim: The predictive capacity of FCθ was formally mediated by the effect of FCθ on the rate of second-order evidence accumulation.
source: Third, this predictive capacity was formally mediated by the effect of FCθ on the rate of second-order evidence accumulation, as indexed by CPP build-up rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: FCθ correlated across-subjects with a model-based estimate of the strength of the evidence that fed into the error detection process.
source: Fourth, FCθ correlated across-subjects with a model-based estimate of the strength of the evidence that fed into the error detection process.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis between FCθ and drift ratio shown in Figure 6e.

claim: θ-band activity in pMFC signals the degree to which competing action plans are simultaneously activated, commonly known as 'conflict'.
source: Extensive data suggest that θ-band activity in pMFC signals the degree to which competing action plans are simultaneously activated, commonly known as 'conflict' (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014; Cavanagh et al., 2011; Cohen, 2014; 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on pMFC theta activity.

claim: A post-commitment conflict signal alone would provide a reliable basis for error detection because its magnitude scales with error likelihood and can reliably classify trial-to-trial performance accuracy.
source: Computational models have shown that a post-commitment conflict signal alone would provide a reliable basis for error detection because its magnitude scales with error likelihood and can reliably classify trial-to-trial performance accuracy (Yeung et al., 2004; see also Charles et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claim: The mediation of the FCθ/RTd relationship by CPP build-up rate was partial.
source: Consistent with such a non-specific influence on the post-decisional process, we found that the mediation of the FCθ/RTd relationship by CPP build-up rate was partial, indicating that pMFC may have also influenced the speed of error detection independently of its effect on the rate of evidence accumulation – perhaps via effects on other parameters of the decision process like the response threshold (Cavanagh et al., 2011) or motor execution time.
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: A post-response centro-parietal ERP, labeled the Error Positivity (Pe), reliably discriminates between detected and undetected errors.
source: A substantial literature has already investigated error-related electrophysiological signals in human subjects and highlighted in particular a post-response centro-parietal ERP, labeled the Error Positivity (Pe), that reliably discriminates between detected and undetected errors (Murphy et al., 2012; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001; O'Connell et al., 2007; Overbeek et al., 2005; Ridderinkhof et al., 2009; Wessel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on the Pe component.

claim: Pe amplitude correlates with confidence in perceptual decisions.
source: Although a series of recent studies have demonstrated that Pe amplitude correlates with confidence in perceptual decisions (Boldt and Yeung, 2015) and the criterion that subjects impose on error detection reports (Steinhauser and Yeung, 2010) and have thereby associated this component with the general quality of the metacognitive decision process [see also Steinhauser and Yeung (2012)], these studies could not identify the Pe with a specific neural mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on the Pe component.

claim: The post-decisional CPP encodes a second-order decision variable that bears precisely the same dynamical properties as have been reported for first-order decision signals in single-unit and population-level neurophysiology.
source: The present study, by contrast, demonstrates that the post-decisional CPP encodes a second-order decision variable that bears precisely the same dynamical properties as have been reported for first-order decision signals in single-unit and population-level neurophysiology, including an RT-predictive build-up rate and a boundary-crossing relationship to response execution – properties that have never been previously reported for the Pe.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the key findings of the study regarding CPP dynamics.

claim: The pre-decision build-up of the CPP encompasses activity that has traditionally been associated with the classic P300 or 'P3b'.
source: Where we have previously demonstrated that the pre-decision build-up of the CPP encompasses activity that has traditionally been associated with the classic P300 or 'P3b' (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015), an important implication of the present findings is that the post-decision build-up of the CPP corresponds to the activity commonly attributed to the Pe.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: The post-decision build-up of the CPP corresponds to the activity commonly attributed to the Pe.
source: Where we have previously demonstrated that the pre-decision build-up of the CPP encompasses activity that has traditionally been associated with the classic P300 or 'P3b' (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; O'Connell et al., 2012; Twomey et al., 2015), an important implication of the present findings is that the post-decision build-up of the CPP corresponds to the activity commonly attributed to the Pe.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the current findings and previous work.

claim: The P3b and Pe reflect distinct stages of the same neurophysiological process.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the P3b and Pe reflect distinct stages of the same neurophysiological process and point to a unifying mechanistic framework for understanding both signals.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that both pre- and post-decision CPP dynamics reflect evidence accumulation.

claim: EEG data were acquired using an ActiveTwo system (BioSemi, The Netherlands) from 64 scalp electrodes.
source: Continuous EEG was acquired using an ActiveTwo system (BioSemi, The Netherlands) from 64 scalp electrodes, configured to the standard 10/20 setup and digitized at 512 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methods used for data acquisition.

claim: Eye-blinks and other noise transients were isolated and removed from the EEG data via independent component analysis (ICA).
source: Eye-blinks and other noise transients were isolated and removed from the EEG data via independent component analysis (ICA).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the preprocessing methods used.

claim: All EEG data were converted to current source density to increase spatial selectivity and minimize volume conduction.
source: Lastly, all EEG data were converted to current source density (Kayser and Tenke, 2006) to increase spatial selectivity and minimize volume conduction (Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; Twomey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a preprocessing step with citations supporting its purpose.

claim: Analysis of Go-trial dynamics was restricted to trials with primary RTs > 350 ms.
source: Analysis of Go-trial dynamics was restricted to trials with primary RTs > 350 ms (leading to the exclusion of 17.4 ± 12.1% of trials per subject) because the amplitude of the CPP signal was affected by visual-evoked potentials that coincided with the evolution of the decision-related activity on quicker trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
